name: date
one_line: print or set the system date and time
plain: `date` prints the current date and time in whatever format you ask for, converts between formats, and does date arithmetic (such as 'what is 90 days from now?').
In forensics and CTFs it converts Unix timestamps (seconds since 1970) to readable dates and back, and builds timestamps for logs and filenames.
when: Convert a Unix timestamp such as 1767225600 to a date.
Put a date in a file name: backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz.
Work out how long ago something happened.

examples.title: The current date and time
examples.explain: Prints the date in your locale's default format.

examples.title: A custom format  (+FORMAT)
examples.explain: Format letters: %Y year, %m month, %d day, %H hour, %M minute, %S second, %F is %Y-%m-%d, %T is %H:%M:%S, %s is Unix seconds.

examples.title: Unix timestamp now
examples.explain: Seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. Forensic tools show many times this way.

examples.title: Convert a timestamp to a date  (-d @N)
examples.explain: The @ means 'seconds since the epoch'. Add -u to show UTC instead of your local zone.

examples.title: Show UTC  (-u)
examples.explain: Always use UTC when comparing logs from different machines.

examples.title: Date arithmetic  (-d)
examples.cmd: date -d '90 days ago' +%F; date -d 'next friday' +%F; date -d '2026-11-21 + 2 weeks' +%F
examples.explain: -d understands phrases such as 'yesterday', '3 hours ago' or a date plus an offset.

examples.title: A file's modification time  (-r)
examples.explain: -r prints the last-modified time of a file.

examples.title: Standard formats  (-I, -R, --rfc-3339)
examples.explain: -I gives ISO 8601 (2026-11-14), -R the e-mail style, --rfc-3339 another standard form. These are safe formats for logs.

options.plain: Show the time described by STRING instead of now: @TIMESTAMP, 'yesterday', '2 hours ago'.
Annotate the parsed date and warn about questionable usage.
options.use: Working out why a date string is misread.

options.plain: Process each line of DATEFILE like -d.
Output ISO 8601 form (date, hours, minutes, seconds, ns).
Output an RFC 5322 e-mail date such as Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000.
Show the last modification time of FILE.
Print or set Coordinated Universal Time.
Output the available resolution of timestamps.

mistakes: Unix timestamps in milliseconds (13 digits) need dividing by 1000 before date -d @.
Forgetting the time zone: use -u when comparing logs.
date -d is a GNU feature: macOS date uses -r for timestamps.
Using spaces or colons in file names made from dates: prefer %F_%H%M%S.
